title: Don’t Write Off Quality Stocks

https://www.barrons.com/articles/dont-write-off-quality-stocks-51549050491 Don’t Write Off Quality Stocks By Feb. 1, 2019 2:48 p.m. ET Order Reprints Courtesy Photograph Text size
When the Federal Reserve on Wednesday announced what sounds like the suspension of its interest-rate-hiking cycle, it appeared to be a green light for risk-on factors like high beta and momentum—and another reason for quality stocks to underperform. That might not be the case.
After the S&P 500 bottomed on Dec. 24, the quality factor had been out of favor. The Invesco S&P 500 Quality exchange-traded fund (ticker: SPHQ), whose largest positions include Procter & Gamble (PG) and Apple (AAPL), gained 13.9% through the Jan. 30, the day of the Fed meeting, trailing not only the S&P 500’s 14% rise but also the Invesco S&P 500 Momentum ETF ’s (SPMO) 17.2% advance and the Invesco S&P 500 High Beta ETF ’s (SPHB) 20.9% rise.
That’s to be expected. Though different firms use different measures, the quality factor is made up of companies with low debt levels, consistent cash flow, and stable earnings. Those qualities are just the kind of thing you look for when markets feel a bit iffy, not when the S&P 500 has just suffered a near-bear market and is rapidly bouncing back. That’s when high-beta stocks—those that are most volatile relative to the market—would be expected to shine. Newsletter Sign-up
The Fed meeting shouldn’t have changed that. The central bank, after all, said it would stop raising interest rates for now—and even that, if necessary, it could stop shrinking its balance sheet. Since the meeting, though, quality has gotten a lift. The Invesco S&P 500 Quality ETF gained 1.7% from Jan. 30 through Feb. 2, outpacing the S&P 500’s 1.3% rise.
“Quality stocks can still perform well in this market and post-Fed,” Christopher Harvey, head of equity and quant strategy at Wells Fargo Securities, told Barron’s.
That the quality factor is finding favor despite the Fed’s actions isn’t as much of a puzzle as it might seem. Quality stocks do better when rates are rising because their lower debt loads are less onerous to finance. The Fed said it would be patient before hiking again, which should favor riskier companies. But the federal-funds futures market is implying that the Fed’s patience has a limit. Before the meeting, the market was suggesting a 0% chance of a rate hike in June. Since then, the odds have increased to 7%.
That’s no surprise, given the economic strength revealed by Friday’s payrolls report—the U.S. added 304,000 jobs in January—and the jump in the Institute for Supply Management’s manufacturing index. When it comes to the quality factor, the dovish Fed “maybe slows it down a bit, but as a longer-term theme, we think it’s still intact,” Savita Subramanian, chief U.S. equity strategist at Bank of America Merrill Lynch, told Barron’s in an email.
Quality also performs better in periods of higher volatility, Subramanian says. She notes that it tends to outperform when the Cboe Volatility Index, or VIX, rises above 25, while low-quality and momentum underperform.
The VIX fell to 16.6 this week, down from its December peak of just over 37—and would anyone be surprised if its spiked again? While investors don’t appear to worry about the Fed tightening the U.S. economy into a recession, uncertainty still prevails globally. China’s economy continues to slow, despite its efforts to stimulate growth, while Europe could be hitting stall speed. And new tariffs could still be in the offing, despite the seeming progress that the U.S. and China have been making on trade.
That wouldn’t be all that different from another period when high-quality outperformed. From 1995 to 1998, the VIX doubled and the S&P 500 returned 80%, led by high-quality stocks, Subramanian notes.
And we remember how that ended.
